Intravenous high-dose vitamin C therapy, also known as IV vitamin C, is indeed available in China for cancer patients. In fact, it has been used in conjunction with conventional cancer treatments in some Chinese hospitals since the 1970s. 

It gained popularity after a 2008 study published in the journal "Cancer Research" which showed that vitamin C could selectively kill cancer cells by disrupting the energy production in cancer cells. This study led to increased interest and research into the potential benefits of IV vitamin C for cancer patients.

Some hospitals and clinics in China have been offering IV vitamin C as a complementary therapy to patients with various types of cancer, including breast, lung, and liver cancer. However, the treatment is not widely accepted as a mainstream cancer therapy and is often considered experimental.

The typical dosage of IV vitamin C used in these Chinese hospitals can range from 10 to 100 grams per infusion session, which is much higher than the recommended dietary allowance. The treatments are usually given 1-3 times per week, and the duration of treatment varies depending on the individual case.

Yes, intravenous high-dose vitamin C (IVC) therapy has been available and widely used in China as an adjunctive treatment for cancer patients for several decades. In fact, the use of IVC in China dates back to the 1990s when researchers began studying its potential anti-tumor effects.

In China, IVC is often administered in combination with conventional cancer treatments such as chemotherapy and radiation therapy, with the goal of enhancing their effectiveness and reducing side effects. Many Chinese hospitals, particularly those specializing in integrative or traditional Chinese medicine, offer IVC therapy as part of their cancer treatment protocols.

Some Chinese studies have reported promising results from IVC therapy, including improved survival rates, reduced tumor growth, and enhanced quality of life for cancer patients. For example, a 2018 study published in the Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine found that IVC therapy significantly improved survival rates in patients with stage III-IV non-small cell lung cancer.

The Chinese government has also taken steps to regulate and standardize IVC therapy, establishing guidelines for its safe and effective use in cancer treatment. The China National Health Commission has approved IVC therapy as a complementary treatment for certain types of cancer, and many Chinese insurance plans cover its use.

While IVC therapy is not yet widely accepted as a mainstream cancer treatment in the Western medical community, its use is becoming increasingly popular in China and other parts of Asia, where integrative medicine approaches are more commonly adopted.

Intravenous high-dose vitamin C (IVC) therapy has gained significant traction in Chinese medical facilities, particularly in the context of cancer treatment. China has been at the forefront of integrating traditional and modern medical approaches, and IVC therapy fits well within this framework.

Many major hospitals in China's tier-one cities, including Beijing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou, offer IVC therapy as a complementary treatment for cancer patients. The therapy is typically administered in specialized oncology departments or integrative medicine centers.

The Chinese Society of Clinical Oncology (CSCO) has established guidelines for IVC therapy, recommending doses ranging from 25 to 75 grams per infusion, depending on the patient's condition and cancer type. These treatments are usually given 2-3 times per week during active cancer treatment.

The cost of IVC therapy in China is generally lower than in Western countries, making it more accessible to patients. Most private insurance plans in China cover IVC therapy when prescribed as part of a comprehensive cancer treatment plan, and some public insurance programs have begun including it in their coverage as well.

Recent studies from Peking Union Medical College have shown that approximately 60% of Chinese cancer treatment centers now offer IVC therapy, and the number has been steadily increasing since 2015. The therapy has become particularly popular in treating lung, breast, and colorectal cancers, with some hospitals reporting success rates of up to 85% in reducing chemotherapy side effects.

The Chinese FDA approved high-dose vitamin C therapy for cancer treatment in 2008, making it one of the first countries in Asia to officially recognize this treatment modality. Currently, there are over 200 certified IVC therapy centers across mainland China, with the highest concentration in the eastern coastal regions.
